Eighth grade science · Unit 8.7

Stars, Galaxies & the Universe

The Sun is just one star among about 200 billion in our galaxy, and our galaxy is one among trillions. After Unit 8.6: Gravity, Orbits and the Solar System and Unit 7.8: The Electromagnetic Spectrum (starlight is how we learn about stars), we zoom out to the biggest scales. Astronomers cannot touch stars, so they rely on evidence and models, the heart of Unit 0: How Science Works.

Where we left off: Unit 8.6 covered our Solar System, and Unit 7.8 showed that starlight carries information. You may already have learned that the Sun is a star. Now we zoom out: how stars shine and die, how galaxies are arranged, and how the universe began.

Concept 1 · Fusion factories

Stars shine by fusing atoms

A star is a giant ball of gas held together by gravity. In its core, nuclear fusion joins hydrogen into helium, releasing huge energy. Apparent brightness depends on true luminosity and distance.

A star is a huge, hot ball of gas, mostly hydrogen and helium. Its own gravity pulls the gas inward and squeezes the center to extremely high temperature and pressure. There, nuclear fusion forces hydrogen nuclei together to make helium, and a little mass turns into a lot of energy. That energy flows out and makes the star shine. Luminosity is the total light energy a star gives off each second. Apparent brightness is how bright it looks from Earth, and it gets dimmer with distance, so a distant powerful star can look fainter than a nearby weak one. Our Sun is the nearest star, about 150 million km (93 million miles) away.

Analogy

Headlights in the dark

A car's headlight looks bright up close and a faint dot far away, though it is the same lamp. A star's brightness works the same way.

Concept 2 · Born, live, die

A star's mass decides its life

Stars form in nebulae, spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen (main sequence), then swell and die. Big stars live fast and die young in supernovas; small stars live long.

A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space. Gravity can pull part of it together until its center is hot enough for fusion, and a star is born. For most of its life a star is on the main sequence, steadily fusing hydrogen into helium. The more mass a star has, the hotter its core, and the faster it burns its fuel, so heavy stars shine brighter but live a much shorter time (millions of years) than small ones (many billions). When the hydrogen runs low the star swells into a giant. A massive star ends in an explosion called a supernova; a star like the Sun sheds its outer layers and leaves a small, hot white dwarf. Heavier elements made in stars are spread by these deaths.

Analogy

Cars and gas tanks

A sports car burns its tank in hours; a small hybrid sips fuel for days. Massive stars burn fuel so fast they last only millions of years.

Real world

The full story: where the atoms in you came from

  1. 13.8 billion years ago: the Big Bang. The universe began extremely hot and dense, and it has been expanding and cooling ever since. For the first few minutes it was hot enough to fuse protons and neutrons together. By about 20 minutes it had made everything it ever would make by itself: about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium (by mass), plus a trace of lithium. Then it was too cool and thin to fuse anything more. So at this point there was no carbon, no oxygen, no iron, no rock, and nothing alive. Only the lightest elements existed.
  2. 380,000 years: the first atoms, and the first light. Until now the universe was a hot, glowing fog. Then it cooled enough for electrons to join the nuclei, and light could finally travel freely. That light is still arriving today. It is the cosmic microwave background (CMB), described in Concept 5.
  3. About 100 to 200 million years: the first stars. Gravity pulled clumps of hydrogen and helium together until their cores were hot enough for fusion. These first stars were mostly very massive, so they lived only a few million years.
  4. Inside stars: building new elements. Every star fuses hydrogen into helium. Red giants and massive stars go further: helium fuses into carbon and oxygen, and the biggest stars keep going, making neon, magnesium and silicon, and ending with iron. Iron is the end of the line, because fusing iron takes energy instead of giving it off.
  5. Supernovas: spreading the atoms. When a massive star's iron core can no longer hold the star up, the core collapses and the star blows apart as a supernova. The blast makes still more elements and scatters everything into space. Sun-sized stars add carbon and nitrogen by puffing off their outer layers late in life. Elements heavier than iron, like gold and uranium, come from the extreme conditions of supernovas and of colliding neutron stars (a 2017 collision was seen in both gravitational waves and light).
  6. Recycling for billions of years. New stars form from gas that earlier stars enriched, make more elements, and die in their turn. How many supernovas did it take? Nobody can count them exactly. In a galaxy like ours a massive star explodes about once every 50 to 100 years. Over the roughly 9 billion years before the Sun was born, that adds up to something on the order of a hundred million supernovas in the Milky Way alone, plus the winds of countless smaller stars.
  7. 4.6 billion years ago: our Solar System. A cloud enriched by many generations of earlier stars collapsed to make the Sun and planets. Even then only about 1 to 2% of it was heavier than helium. That small slice became all the rock and metal of Earth, the oxygen in air and water, and the carbon in living things.
  8. You. Most of the hydrogen in your body (the H in H₂O) was made in the Big Bang. The carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, calcium and iron were made in stars that lived and died before the Sun existed. We really are star stuff.

Concept 3 · The H-R diagram

Plot temperature against brightness

Plot luminosity against temperature and stars fall into groups: a diagonal main sequence, bright giants at the top, faint white dwarfs at the bottom. This is called the Hertzsprung–Russell (H-R) diagram.

Astronomers sort stars using two measurements: surface temperature, which shows as color (blue-white stars are hotter than red ones), and luminosity, the total light given off. On the Hertzsprung–Russell (H-R) diagram, each star is a dot, with temperature along the bottom (hotter on the left, by convention) and luminosity up the side. Most stars fall along a diagonal band, the main sequence. Cool but very luminous stars (red giants and supergiants) are large, so they sit at the top right, while hot but dim white dwarfs are small and sit at the bottom left. A star's position tells you its type and stage of life.

Analogy

A class height-weight chart

Plot height against weight for a class and you see a clear trend and a few outliers. Stars show the same kind of pattern.

Concept 4 · Cities of stars

Galaxies are huge star collections

A galaxy is billions of stars, gas, and dust bound by gravity. Our Milky Way is a spiral about 100,000 light-years across. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year.

A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity. Galaxies come in shapes such as spiral, elliptical and irregular. Our Sun is one of a few hundred billion stars in the Milky Way. Space distances are so large that astronomers use the light-year, the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km (5.88 trillion miles). Because light takes time to travel, looking at a far-off object means seeing it as it was when the light left: the Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away, so we see it as it was 2.5 million years ago.

Analogy

Looking back in time

Light takes time to arrive. When you see a star 100 light-years away, you see it as it was 100 years ago.

Straight talk

Will people ever travel to the stars?

Almost certainly not. This is not a lack of trying: it comes from the size of space and from the rules of the universe.

  • The distances are enormous. The nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is 4.24 light-years away, about 40 trillion km. Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object, travels about 17 km/s. At that speed it would need roughly 75,000 years to cover the distance. Even the Parker Solar Probe, the fastest spacecraft ever (about 190 km/s, only while falling past the Sun), would take around 6,700 years.
  • Going faster costs more and more energy. To cross the gap within a human lifetime a ship would need a large fraction of the speed of light. But the closer an object gets to light speed, the more energy each extra bit of speed takes, and the energy needed grows without limit. (Older books say the object's mass increases as it speeds up. Physicists today prefer to say its energy and momentum grow, but the conclusion is the same.) Nothing that has mass can ever reach the speed of light.
  • Even a slow trip is out of reach. Pushing a 100-tonne ship to just 10% of light speed takes about as much energy as the whole world uses in about a month, for the push alone, with no fuel and no braking to stop at the other end. Rocket fuel for that would weigh far more than the ship.
  • People are fragile. A decades-long trip needs food, air, water and shielding from deadly cosmic rays, and a speck of dust hitting a ship at that speed hits like a bomb.
Voyager 1 (17 km/s)
75,000 years
Parker Solar Probe (190 km/s)
6,700 yr

Travel time to Proxima Centauri (4.24 light-years) at each probe’s top speed. Even the fastest craft ever built would need thousands of years.

So here is the honest summary: with everything we know about physics, crewed trips to other stars look out of reach for any technology we can reasonably imagine. We will keep exploring the Solar System with people and robots, and we study the stars the only way possible: by catching their light. Scientists do dream about tiny robotic probes pushed by lasers, but those are still only ideas. Never say never in science, but this is the straight answer.

Concept 5 · Big Bang

The universe is expanding

Distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster they recede. Running the film backward points to a Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago. Leftover glow (CMB) is more evidence.

Light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths, shifting it toward red (redshift), which tells us they are moving away. In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that farther galaxies recede faster, a pattern called Hubble's law. This does not mean we are at the center: space itself is expanding, so every galaxy moves away from every other. If the expansion is run backward, everything was once much hotter and denser, which is the Big Bang model. A second line of evidence is the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint microwave radiation coming from all directions, thought to be the leftover glow of the early hot universe.

Analogy

Raisin bread rising

As dough rises, every raisin moves away from every other raisin, and farther raisins move away faster. No raisin is the center.

Deeper

What are we really seeing in the CMB?

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the oldest light there is. Here is what it is, and why we can see it.

  • A fog that cleared. For the first 380,000 years the universe was so hot that atoms could not hold together. Free electrons scattered light in every direction, so the universe was an opaque glowing fog, like looking at the inside of a cloud. Then it cooled to about 3,000 degrees, electrons joined nuclei to make neutral atoms, and the fog cleared. Light set off in straight lines everywhere at once.
  • Old light, stretched. That light was bright orange-white at first. But as it crossed space, the space itself kept stretching, by about 1,100 times, and the light waves stretched with it. Orange light became microwaves, the same kind your microwave oven uses, and the glow cooled to just 2.7 degrees above absolute zero. It is the redshift idea applied to the whole universe.
  • It comes from every direction. We are not at a special place. Light that was released everywhere is arriving everywhere. We are seeing the edge of the fog, a sphere around us, at the distance from which light has just had time to reach us. (The matter that gave off that light is now about 46 billion light-years away, because space kept expanding while the light traveled.)
  • A baby picture. The CMB is almost perfectly smooth, but there are tiny hot and cold patches, about 1 part in 100,000. They show where matter was a little denser. Gravity pulled on those patches for hundreds of millions of years and grew them into galaxies. The colors on the map are exaggerated so we can see the patches.
  • Why we cannot see earlier. Before the fog cleared, light could not travel far, so the CMB is the farthest back that any light can take us.
  • Found by accident. In 1964 two radio engineers, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, could not get rid of a faint hiss in their antenna, even after cleaning it out (pigeon droppings included). It turned out to be the CMB that Big Bang scientists had predicted. Its spectrum matches a perfect glow of 2.725 degrees better than anything else ever measured.
Deeper

How to think about light from far away

  • Looking far away is looking back in time. Light travels at a fixed speed, so it takes time to arrive. You see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago, the nearest star as it was 4 years ago, the Andromeda galaxy as it was about 2.5 million years ago, and the farthest galaxies in the Hubble deep field as they were over 13 billion years ago.
  • We never see the present. There is no picture of how the universe looks “right now”. Every telescope shows an older and older movie the farther it looks.
  • Space stretched while the light was on its way. A galaxy whose light has been traveling 13 billion years is now much farther away than 13 billion light-years, and its light has been stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. That stretching is the redshift in Hubble's law.
  • The observable universe. We can only see things whose light has had time to reach us since the Big Bang. Beyond that there is more universe, but its light has not arrived yet. It is a limit of time, not an edge of space.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A friend says "if all galaxies are moving away from us, we must be at the center of the universe." Use the raisin bread analogy and the Hubble data to explain why that does not follow.

Show a model answer

In an expanding universe, every galaxy sees all the others moving away, with farther ones receding faster, just like every raisin in rising dough. Hubble's straight-line relation (speed proportional to distance) is what we expect from uniform expansion. No place is the center.

Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): balloons and a marker (expanding universe), raisin bread dough or a stretchy rubber band with dots, a flashlight and a ruler (inverse square), graph paper, a toy spectroscope or diffraction glasses, a photo of the H-R diagram.

  • Concept 1: Draw dots on a balloon, inflate it, and measure distances before and after.
  • Concept 2: Shine a flashlight on graph paper at 10, 20, and 40 cm and count squares lit.
  • Concept 3: Plot 15 stars on an H-R diagram from a table.
  • Concept 4: View lamps through diffraction glasses and compare spectra.
  • Concept 5: Build a 1-meter-per-AU solar system, then find where the next star would be (about 270 km!).

Common misconceptions:

  • "The Big Bang was an explosion in space." It was an expansion of space.
  • "The Sun is a typical big star." It is average-sized.
  • "Stars live forever." They have lifecycles.
  • "We see stars as they are now." We see them as they were.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: teach evidence ranking: expansion, redshift, CMB, element abundance (Unit 0), and why a scientific theory is a tested explanation, not a guess.
